messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: L-BFGS
parts:
Quick question for everyone.  I'm considering implementing the limited memory version of BFGS in Stan.  The question is whether we would prefer this as a "new" algorithm (i.e., the users could set algorithm=bfgs or algorithm=lbfgs (or maybe algorithm=bfgs hessian_approx=limited) or simply as a drop-in replacement for BFGS.

The argument for the drop-in replacement is that, honestly, there's not a lot of reason to use BFGS if L-BFGS is available.  In general L-BFGS works better than BFGS and uses *much* less memory.  The flip side is that it's easy enough to have both just in case someone wanted to use BFGS instead.

I realize that most people may not care about this, but I thought I would check in before I got started.  Thoughts?

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: L-BFGS
parts:
Nocedal and Wright

http://download.springer.com.ezproxy.cul.columbia.edu/static/pdf/264/chp%253A10.1007%252F978-0-387-40065-5_7.pdf?auth66=1383700937_ddec5bba9ea5a1994ae00038b73a436a&ext=.pdf

claims on page 180 that "The main weakness of the L-BFGS method is that it converges slowly on ill-conditioned problems—specifically, on problems where the Hessian matrix contains a wide distribution of eigenvalues." This is basically the same deal as strong Wolfe vs. weak Wolfe: I don't know how we can presume that the user has a well-conditioned / non-degenerate / etc. problem, particularly if someone is using it for some arbitrary optimization problem as opposed to finding a posterior mode or whatever.

So, I think we should have options. The documentation of L-BFGS is basically the same as the documentation of BFGS with about 1 additional option.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: L-BFGS
parts:
I don't think L-BFGS dominates BFGS or vice versa, even within a particular class of optimization problems. Also, you wouldn't necessarily know if the Hessian were ill-conditioned until you solve the problem. In the chapter on limited memory methods, Nocedal and Wright are only comparing L-BFGS to other limited memory methods. I don't remember them ever comparing L-BFGS to BFGS because the main difference between them is that L-BFGS is simply necessary when your optimization problem has so many parameters that the machine doesn't have enough RAM to do BFGS.

But in the BFGS chapter

http://download.springer.com.ezproxy.cul.columbia.edu/static/pdf/265/chp%253A10.1007%252F978-0-387-40065-5_6.pdf?auth66=1383747383_b6da37dfd810ad1d77e52760cb0ffce8&ext=.pdf

they do talk about the ability of BFGS to self-correct within a few iterations if the Hessian approximation strays. Also, at some point during the process, BFGS achieves better than linear convergence on well-behaved problems, whereas I think L-BFGS is linear throughout.

Ben

My memory is fuzzy, but I recall seeing comparisons between BFGS and L-BFGS suggesting that, while L-BFGS has a slower theoretical rate of convergence, in practice it can actually converge a little faster, particularly when the curvature of the space varies significantly.  I can't find the paper anymore, but I think this was based on results on the CUTE test problems.  Anyway, I think I will implement both for now.  In fact, it should be straightforward to simply include L-BFGS as an option when running BFGS.  As part of it I'd like to include some tests on the models and we could use that to potentially make a final decision.

Regarding the Newton method, I know I've suggested removing it for the mean time.  The reason isn't so much that the optimization method is bad, but that it's currently computing the Hessian using a finite difference which will be, at best, inefficient.  Once we have higher-order autodiff and the Newton method uses that to get the Hessian, then it's definitely worth having for small to medium sized problems.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: L-BFGS
parts:
It's hard to say anything about the relative speeds of the two
algorithms during search. During convergence, BFGS achieves
superlinear convergence whereas LBFGS only achieves linear
convergence. That is, roughly speaking, –log(distance from optimum)
increases superlinearly with BFGS, whereas it only increases linearly
with LBFGS (same as gradient descent, but with better constants). In
practical terms, this means that if you use BFGS you might as well
wait for it to converge fully (modulo early stopping-type concerns),
whereas you might be waiting a very long time for LBFGS to converge to
10 digits of accuracy or whatever.

Matt

It's hard to say anything about the relative speeds of the two
algorithms during search. During convergence, BFGS achieves
superlinear convergence whereas LBFGS only achieves linear
convergence. That is, roughly speaking, –log(distance from optimum)
increases superlinearly with BFGS, whereas it only increases linearly
with LBFGS (same as gradient descent, but with better constants). In
practical terms, this means that if you use BFGS you might as well
wait for it to converge fully (modulo early stopping-type concerns),
whereas you might be waiting a very long time for LBFGS to converge to
10 digits of accuracy or whatever.

Matt

On 11/8/13, 3:08 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
Agreed, in theory there is little to be said about search.  I am basing my assessment on empirical results on a number
of test problems.  I'm not sure which paper I'm remembering, but poking around turned up
http://www.ece.northwestern.edu/~nocedal/PDFfiles/limited-memory.pdf (see table 4 on page 8).  I wish I could find the
1988 tech report they reference, as it seems likely to have more results.

Ben, thanks for posting a list of the problems having issues with optimization.  I'll take a look and see what's
happening with them.

We know some of them aren't going to work in practice
because there are no modes.

If it's possible and not too much work, it'd be great to diagnose that
in the same way that the sampler diagnoses an improper posterior.

It should be possible.  Basically, if it stops optimizing due to a small change in objective value or small move in parameter space and the gradient is still large it probably means the function is unbounded and has no mode.  (It could also be a bug, an error in the gradient or an objective with extremely bad curvature, but those are less likely.)

And by the way, Daniel and I have been using the optimizer
for the diff-eq models we've been developing and it's awesome.
The sampler takes about 10 minutes times 4 chains to generate 100
or so effective samples using the non-hierarchial model, whereas
the optimizer runs in about 30 seconds.  This is just auto-diffing
a non-stiff integrator so far.

Glad to hear it's useful for you guys!  It was very much me scratching my own itch...the beauty of open source :)

Cheers,
Marcus

On Tue, Nov 5, 2013 at 7:25 PM, Matt Hoffman <mdho...@cs.princeton.edu> wrote:
It's hard to say anything about the relative speeds of the two
algorithms during search. During convergence, BFGS achieves
superlinear convergence whereas LBFGS only achieves linear
convergence. That is, roughly speaking, –log(distance from optimum)
increases superlinearly with BFGS, whereas it only increases linearly
with LBFGS (same as gradient descent, but with better constants). In
practical terms, this means that if you use BFGS you might as well
wait for it to converge fully (modulo early stopping-type concerns),
whereas you might be waiting a very long time for LBFGS to converge to
10 digits of accuracy or whatever.

Matt

> >>> It's hard to say anything about the relative speeds of the two
> >>> algorithms during search. During convergence, BFGS achieves
> >>> superlinear convergence whereas LBFGS only achieves linear
> >>> convergence. That is, roughly speaking, –log(distance from optimum)
> >>> increases superlinearly with BFGS, whereas it only increases linearly
> >>> with LBFGS (same as gradient descent, but with better constants). In
> >>> practical terms, this means that if you use BFGS you might as well
> >>> wait for it to converge fully (modulo early stopping-type concerns),
> >>> whereas you might be waiting a very long time for LBFGS to converge to
> >>> 10 digits of accuracy or whatever.

> >>> Matt

> >>> On Mon, Nov 4, 2013 at 9:57 AM, Marcus Brubaker
> >>> <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>>> My memory is fuzzy, but I recall seeing comparisons between BFGS and L-BFGS
> >>>> suggesting that, while L-BFGS has a slower theoretical rate of convergence,
> >>>> in practice it can actually converge a little faster, particularly when the
> >>>> curvature of the space varies significantly. I can't find the paper
> >>>> anymore, but I think this was based on results on the CUTE test problems.
> >>>> Anyway, I think I will implement both for now. In fact, it should be
> >>>> straightforward to simply include L-BFGS as an option when running BFGS. As
> >>>> part of it I'd like to include some tests on the models and we could use
> >>>> that to potentially make a final decision.
> >>>>
> >>>> Regarding the Newton method, I know I've suggested removing it for the mean
> >>>> time. The reason isn't so much that the optimization method is bad, but
> >>>> that it's currently computing the Hessian using a finite difference which
> >>>> will be, at best, inefficient. Once we have higher-order autodiff and the
> >>>> Newton method uses that to get the Hessian, then it's definitely worth
> >>>> having for small to medium sized problems.
> >>>>
> >>>> Cheers,

> >>>>>>

> >>>>>> > basically the same deal as strong Wolfe vs. weak Wolfe: I don't

> >>>>>> optimization
> >>>>>> > problem as opposed to finding a posterior mode or whatever.

> >>>>>> Is BFGS better behaved? I didn't see a direct comparison.

> >>>>>> Also, given that we're doing positive-definite Hessian

> >>>>>> BFGS with
> >>>>>> > about 1 additional option.

> >>>>>> The effort's not in the original doc or even in the initial
